#6614. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6613. Best Men’s Winter Parkas 2026: 17 Heavy-Duty Snow-Busting Coats

The best men's parka is a lot like an upright sleeping bag, except it doesn't simply keep you insulated. It also protects your frostbite-prone fits from Mother Nature’s icy clutches, and keeps you looking sharp in the process. Don't believe us? Just ask the parka's most loyal servant: Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher.

Before giving you our favourites, some quick history: Parkas originated in the Arctic, where the Inuit designed them to withstand bone-chilling temperatures. They then made their way to the US military with the introduction of the N-3B parka in the 1950s. Throughout its evolution, the parka's mission has remained unchanged: to keep not just your torso warm, but your thighs and rear end too. Seriously, you've already worn that waist-length puffer to death: Make like Justin Jefferson. Go long.

The North Face McMurdo down parka isn’t just another winter coat—it’s a cold-weather icon with Antarctic-level credibility. Named after McMurdo Station, the US research hub in Antarctica, this parka is designed to thrive in below-freezing temperatures while keeping you comfortable and protected. With 600-fill recycled down insulation and windproof, waterproof, and breathable DryVent technology, it’s eco-friendly armor for the tundra—or the Target parking lot. Made from recycled nylon and polyester, it’s part of The North Face’s recycled-repurpose collection, combining sustainability with serious performance.

Loaded with features like six exterior pockets, a removable faux-fur ruff, an adjustable hood, and a draft flap, this 3.5-pound powerhouse is your portable fortress of warmth. Stylish touches like the midnight petrol color elevate it above standard winter fare, while practical details make it indispensable for everything from scraping windshields to tackling arctic adventures. Whether you’re braving brutal weather or commuting in comfort, the McMurdo is built to last—complete with The North Face’s warranty to keep it in the game longer than your ever-disappearing gloves.

Mountain Hardwear has been a staple in the outdoor gear world long before its sold-out collaboration with Stüssy (though they’ve probably gained a few new fans in the process). Founded in 1993 in Richmond, California, the brand spun off from the well-known outdoor company Sierra Designs. A group of designers and engineers left Sierra Designs to create Mountain Hardwear, and 32 years later, it’s still famous for its technical outerwear, sleeping bags, and pioneering use of Gore-Tex.

This jacket is built for camping, featuring a durable ripstop shell and 650-fill down. With a fully adjustable insulated hood and a drawcord at the waist to trap in heat, it’s tough to top even before you encounter the two BYO-bevvy pockets—specially designed to carry your favorite beverages. Whether you're in your tent or Air Streamer, this jacket keeps you warm—and your drinks cold—so you can stay cozy and hydrated in style.

Woolrich: So good it doesn't need a logo patch. The American outdoor company was founded in 1830, and since then has become the destination for warmth-minded men who don't need anyone else to know they're walking around in the very best materials.

Which isn't to say this parka won't turn some heads. New for this season, it comes in seven colors, from a stunning light blue to nutty falcon brown, and also boasts some envy-inducing hand-warmer pockets, hidden rib-knit cuffs, and even a water-repellent finish. (A nice touch for a style that typically is more preoccupied with keeping out the cold than the wet.) One more thing: It's called the Cloud because it's incredibly light, even with a 90/10 duck down fill. A winter coat that wears like a summer-weight hoodie? Worth the investment.

This is the kind of Canada Goose jacket that reminds you why the brand is so much more than just a status symbol for finance guys. (Though I'm sure they don't mind being that too.) For one, it's done away with that ubiquitous blue and red logo, and replaced it with a more understated, tonal patch. But that's actually the only thing that's been stripped back here: Otherwise, this parka is packed full of features, from ribbed knit cuffs, to pockets everywhere you look, to a bevy of insulation considerations, from the 625 Fill Down interior all the way to the soft, lined chin guard—a nice touch.

Available this season in Black, Olive, and Desert Sand (above), it's backed by Canada Goose's lifetime guarantee. So, yes, you're spending a fortune. But the brand stands ready to make sure you'll never need to buy another parka again.

The Japanese label FrizmWORKS has reimagined a classic, ‘60s‐era expedition parka silhouette—quilted down, hard-wearing cotton-blend shell, boxy hooded cut—and, sixty years later, given it a whole new life. From the tonal matte finish to the utilitarian drawcord hem, this is a mountain‐camp relic reimagined for your 2025 commute. It’s rugged without resorting to SSX Tricky branding, and along with the requisite down filling also has two fun, unexpected and large pockets on the back. It also comes in a joyful orange color, if that black is a little too subtle for you.

I can't be the only one who was excited to see Reigning Champ get back into making real clothes. (Though, let’s be honest, the brand’s sweatsuits are still some of my favorites.) But this high-powered, goose-filled nylon parka? It's built for Canadian winters, which means it’ll easily thrive anywhere else, too. Technically, that means 700 fill power down, and a weather-repellent nylon shell to keep out wind and rain, as well as the colder temps. Its defining feature is its stealthy, all-black appearance, and Reigning Champ has leant hard into that vibe, with hidden interior pockets, concealed rib cuffs, and a shock cord hood that you can pull as tight as you like. Now you see me, now you don't.

The new kids on the parka block, Big Rock Candy Mountaineering, are bringing the fun back with their vibrant, winter parka colors. These extreme cold-weather parkas take inspiration from mid-century American outdoor brands. Can’t think of any off the top of your head? Skim through a book like this, and you’ll catch the vibe.

BRCM’s parkas are packed with cozy duck down and feature a 100% grosgrain shell. This ribbed texture, courtesy of its tight weave, makes the fabric tough as nails and resistant to wear and tear. The ginormous pockets? Perfect for stashing your winter accessories (or your snacks). And if the wind has you feeling like it’s got something to prove, just tighten up the drawstring waist, hood, and hem. One of the coolest features? The jacket’s silhouette. When cinched, you can clasp your bag around the waist—ideal for those who love a good backpacking adventure. Although BRCM is still a fresh face in the outerwear world, it already feels like an instant classic.

Getting your hands on one of the first-ever parkas is basically impossible—right up there with finding your keys when you’re already late. Enter The Real McCoy’s, which somehow pulls it off with museum-grade reproductions. Every detail is obsessively dialed, down to the DuPont-developed nylon shell that helped kick off the whole modern-materials era.

Today’s outdoor companies are still trying to capture Patagonia’s lightning-in-a-bottle formula from when the brand first burst onto the scene: Be nice to everyone, make products the right way, and design jackets built to last forever. Take its Glacier parka, for example: it’s weatherproof, cozy enough to double as a sleeping bag, and so comfortable you might consider skipping the tent altogether.

If you’re after a quieter, minimalist parka—and you’ve got the budget—the Therme Parka delivers. It’s hip-length, packed with goose down, and built with the brand’s more environmentally friendly GORE-TEX ePE fabric, meaning it’s primed to handle a lifetime of winters.

The Alpha Industries N-3B is the real-deal snorkel parka—because it is the real deal. Produced early in the company's history in the 1950s, the parka is still tough as nails and loaded with reinforced elbow patches, a full-length storm flap, and snug inset knit cuffs that keep wind firmly in its place.

Founded in 1960, Fjällräven are sort of Sweden's Patagonia. By which we mean they've always thought about three things: High-performance materials, a reasonable enough price point, and dressing it all up in some great primary colors.

Nanga is your favorite outerwear brand’s favorite outerwear brand. Its parka riffs on the US Air Force’s N-3B flight jacket, upgraded with AuroraTex—a high-performance fabric that keeps you dry no matter what. Add handwarmer pockets and a discreet cigar pouch, and you’ve got a parka that nails the perfect blend between utility and style.

Goldwin is so good, it literally owns the North Face in Japan. (Like, literally.) This handsome down parka is wind-blocking, body-warming, and equipped with a PERTEX Quantum ripstop lining (and shell) to prevent the tears and rips that lightweight fabrics can otherwise be prone to.

Berghaus' Meru jacket—which is long enough to qualify as a parka in our book—is packed with retro styling, from the color blocks to the cinchable waistband. 2L Gore-Tex means you could wear it up any peak, but its general aura means you could also wear it up on stage, hands behind your back, tambourine on your head.

Montbell's mastery of lightweight, easy-to-rock, nicely-priced outdoors gear has become its calling card, and it’s on full display here. This down parka is easy to incorporate into pretty much any wardrobe, and even has some nice-looking stitching (which, by the way, the heads call ‘baffling’).

What do you get when you cross a parka with a fireman jacket? A full-scale compliment magnet.

First and foremost: functionality. A great parka should incorporate more features than a midnight infomercial. In the outer shell, you’ll typically find materials like nylon or polyester, and sometimes more rugged options like Gore-Tex. But it's also worth peeking under the hood—literally. Parkas are usually filled with down (duck or goose feathers) or synthetic insulation like polyester. Down is warm and lightweight, but it’s the fair-weather friend of insulation—it falters when wet. Synthetic insulations, on the other hand, is the ride-or-die option, keeping you warm even when soggy.

Hoods are another essential feature. Most will be made of a weatherproof fabric, and some come equipped with fluffy genuine- or faux-fur trims that gently tickle your face with a touch of winter luxury. And then there are the pockets—no one wants to walk around in a blizzard with frozen fingers. (Look for fleece linings.) Finally, asses the length. Longer parkas offer more warmth and protection from the elements, while shorter ones are perfect for commuters who need to dodge frostbite without overheating on the subway.

While function is the defining characteristic of a good parka, a great one should also give your winter fits a serious upgrade. Pair it with a thermal and a chunky sweater for a no-brainer look, or go bold by layering it over a denim jacket, adding corduroys, and anchoring with sturdy boots.

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

#6612. Emma Watson’s Rare Appearance Came With a Vintage Valentino Look

Emma Watson may be keeping a low profile these days, but she hasn’t lost her eye for a good vintage find.

The actress stepped out on Thursday night at GQ’s Men of the Year party in Los Angeles, where she joined guests including Ayo Edebiri, Monica Barbaro, Tinashe, and more at the Chateau Marmont.

For the occasion, Watson wore a vintage patterned piece from Valentino’s collaboration with artist Christi Belcourt for its 2016 resort collection. She paired the colorful design with black-and-white striped Jacquemus stilettos for a lesson in pattern mixing and pairing.

The actress skipped the red carpet arrivals but was photographed outside the venue, staying relatively under the radar despite the star-studded guest list.

The outing marks another occasional appearance from the Harry Potter alum, who has largely stepped away from acting since completing work on Greta Gerwig’s Little Women in 2019. Earlier this month, she attended another Los Angeles event, the LACMA Art+Film Gala, in a sculpted ruby gown.

In a 2025 interview with Hollywood Authentic, Watson spoke about the decision to take a break from the industry, explaining that while she misses the creative process, she doesn’t miss the demands of promoting films.

“I do not miss selling things,” she said, describing that promotional side as “quite soul-destroying,” before adding that she does “very much miss using my skill set, and I very much miss the art.”

Watson has since explored other creative pursuits, including directing and her work on spirits brand Renais, which she co-founded with her brother, Alex. While she hasn’t announced a return to the screen, she has made it clear that she remains open to the right project and intent on being around people who share a passion for film.

“While I might not be making work right now, I still do feel that I’m part of a community,” she said in 2025. “I want to stay connected to that community and be part of it.”

#6610. Mussels With Garlicky Miso Broth

Mussels deserve your attention on weeknights. An affordable and accessible protein, they also happen to cook in less time than it takes to boil water. As the bivalves steam, they release a briny liquid, further perfuming the buttery, sake-fortified miso broth. Load up each bowl with a few good ladles, slurping every drop with an assist from crusty bread or warm rice. And why not enjoy the rest of the bottle of sake alongside your meal?

The seafood counter at your supermarket should sell rinsed and debarred mussels, but it’s easy to do at home. Discard any with cracked shells. Gently tap open raw mussels on a counter to see if they slowly close; if they do, those are okay to use. Swish them in a water-filled salad spinner or colander fitted inside a bowl, draining and refilling until water runs clear (give any especially dirty ones a scrub with a sponge). Use a towel to pull off the fibrous beard and set on a towel-lined tray in the fridge until you’re ready to cook.

More seafood dinners this way: Avgolemono Seafood Stew; Spaghetti alle Vongole; and Gorgeous Green Shrimp.

Place 2 Tbsp. scallions from 8 scallions, thinly sliced on a diagonal, in a small bowl and set aside for serving.

Melt 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter in a large pot over medium heat. Add 8 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining scallions to pot and cook, stirring often, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 2 Tbsp. white miso paste and ½ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes (if using) and cook until miso is broken up and incorporated into butter, about 20 seconds. Pour in 1 cup dry sake or dry white wine and stir to combine, then add 3–3½ lb. mussels, scrubbed, debearded. Cover pot and increase heat to medium-high. Cook, shaking pot occasionally, until mussels open, 5–7 minutes (discard any that do not open). Remove pot from heat.

Squeeze 1 lemon half over mussels. Cut remaining 1 lemon half into wedges for serving. Taste broth and season with kosher salt if needed.

Ladle mussels and broth among shallow bowls, then scatter reserved scallions over. Serve with country-style bread or steamed white rice if desired and lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6607. Butternut Pasta With Sausage and Dates

Squash and sausage are a heroic autumnal pairing, especially in a weeknight-friendly pasta. Butternut is the easiest squash to source—not to mention easily found peeled and chopped (a blessing for those with more timid knife skills). But other winter squash like acorn or red kuri can stand in as desired. Whichever squash you select, a sharp, heavy chef’s knife is best for breaking down the chunky veg. But to make your life easier, microwave the squash for 1 to 2 minutes. It will slightly soften, making it simpler—and safer—to slice through.

Rigatoni’s ribbed surface and large holes help chunky squash sauce cling and bites of seared sausage and date wedge—opting for a nutty whole wheat variety will only add to this meal’s autumnal earthiness.

More cozy pastas this way: Balsamic Mushroom and Sausage Pasta; Creamy Red Curry Pasta; and Baked Feta Pasta With Green Sauce.

Cook 1 medium butternut squash (1½–2 lb.), peeled, halved, seeds removed, cut into 1" pieces (about 6 cups), in a large pot of boiling salted water until very tender, 12–14 minutes. Using a slotted spoon, transfer squash to a medium bowl. Reduce heat to low, cover pot, and leave on burner to keep warm.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium Dutch oven over medium-high. Add 1 lb. hot or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and break up into small pieces with a wooden spoon. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, about 3 minutes. Continue to cook, stirring occasionally, until browned all over and just cooked through, 3–4 minutes more. Transfer to a plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to medium-low. Cook 3½ oz. Medjool dates (about 6), pitted, sliced lengthwise ¾" thick, in same pan, turning halfway though, until deeply browned, 3–4 minutes. Transfer to plate with sausage; season with salt.

Add remaining 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil to pan. Add 6 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and reserved squash. Cook, scraping up browned bits and smashing squash with spoon to break up, until lightly browned and broken up into a chunky paste (pieces do not need to be even), about 5 minutes.

Meanwhile, return cooking liquid in reserved pot to a boil over high heat. Cook 12 oz. short tube pasta (such as rigatoni) until very al dente, about 3 minutes less than package directions (it will finish cooking in sauce). Drain, reserving 3 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid to squash and break up squash with spoon until a saucy consistency. Add pasta, another 1 cup pasta cooking liquid, and reserved sausage and dates. Increase heat to medium-high; cook, adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is al dente and coated in sauce, 2–3 minutes. Remove from heat and stir in 1 Tbsp. sherry vinegar or balsamic vinegar. Taste pasta and add more vinegar, salt and/or pepper if needed.

#6606. Beyoncé Opens Up About How She and Jay-Z Kept Their Intimate Wedding Secret, Even From Guests

Nearly two decades after saying “I do,” Beyoncé is offering a rare glimpse into one of the most private moments of her relationship with Jay-Z. In a new interview with i-D, the singer reflected on their intimate 2008 wedding, revealing that the couple went to great lengths to keep the celebration under wraps.

“We had a very small wedding in our home,” Beyoncé told the publication. “We told the guests we were having a party, and no one knew they were coming to our wedding but our parents and a few friends.”

The couple hosted the ceremony at their New York City residence, and the date they chose (April 4) held special meaning for the pair, with the number four corresponding to both of their birthdays: Beyoncé was born on September 4, while Jay-Z celebrates his on December 4.

Beyoncé also discussed her wedding gown, which was designed by her mother, Tina Knowles. She called it her “favorite dress” that Knowles ever made for her in part because “it was gorgeously simple and made with her love.”

Her mom credited herself in a post celebrating the couple’s anniversary in 2020, saying, “ahem, I designed that dress.”

For the singer, choosing a design by her mother was never about making a fashion statement. “Wearing a dress she designed was very important to me, and more important than any designer dress,” she said.

#6603. Creamy Miso Mushroom Pasta

Mushroom fans: Bookmark this recipe immediately. It will give you everything you want when you crave a creamy mushroom pasta as soon as the crisp fall air sets in. The hardworking trio of miso, Parmesan, and touch of soy sauce delivers an umami bomb of flavor that doesn’t overwhelm, but magnifies, the best of earthy mushrooms. Coupled with luscious noodles enrobed in a creamy (but not heavy) sauce, what’s not to love?

A few helpful notes for pasta success: (1) While any pasta will work, egg-based noodles, like the fettuccine I recommend here, are the best complement to the sauce. The nests (Rummo and De Cecco are great accessible brands) cook far faster than standard straight pasta, almost as fast as fresh. (2) Don’t be afraid to season your mushrooms! Yes, I know this goes against all that we’ve learned about salting them too early in the cooking process, but just a bit of salt will get them going and releasing their water faster for eventual crisp-browned edges. Don’t be alarmed if you see a pool of water at the start of the mushroom cooking—that’s to be expected and just keep going until it evaporates. (3) Don’t forget to reserve plenty of pasta cooking liquid, which is critical to the eventual sauce’s success. I prefer transferring the al dente noodles from the pasta pot to the skillet, letting any residual water come with it (and to ensure you don’t accidentally drain away that liquid gold).

Find more fall favorite meals here: Weeknight Pumpkin Chili; Cream-ish of Mushroom Soup; Mushrooms au Poivre.

Cook 12 oz. egg-based pasta (such as fettuccine nests) in a large pot of boiling salted water, stirring occasionally, until al dente, about 1 minute less than package directions.

Meanwhile, heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet over high. Add 1 lb. crimini or mixed mushrooms (such as button, maitake, oyster, and/or shiitake), sliced ¼" thick or torn into bite-size pieces, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt and toss to coat evenly. Spread out into an even layer and cook, undisturbed, until mushrooms are starting to release their liquid, 2–3 minutes (do not be alarmed; there will be a lot). Continue to cook, tossing occasionally, until moisture is almost completely evaporated and edges of mushrooms are starting to brown, 6–8 minutes.

Reduce heat to medium-high; add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, tossing often, until garlic is fragrant and golden, 1–2 minutes. Pour in ¾ cup dry white wine, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan with a sturdy spatula or flat-edged wooden spoon, and cook until wine is mostly evaporated (you should have about 1 Tbsp. liquid left in pan), about 4 minutes. Reduce heat to medium-low. Add 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 2 Tbsp. white miso and stir until melted and combined. Slowly pour in ½ cup heavy cream, scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan; simmer until thickened slightly, 2–3 minutes. Add 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce; season with freshly ground pepper. Taste and add more salt if needed.

Using tongs, transfer pasta to mushroom mixture and add 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Increase heat to medium and bring to a simmer. Cook, tossing constantly and adding ½–1 cup more pasta cooking liquid to reach desired sauce consistency if needed, until pasta is al dente and liquid has thickened slightly, about 3 minutes.

Remove pan from heat. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup) to pasta and toss to combine. Season generously with more pepper; taste and season with more salt if needed.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan and pepper.

#6602. The Best New Restaurants in New York City to Visit Now

For some New Yorkers, keeping up with the city’s ever-changing restaurant scene is something of a sport. Indeed, there seems to be a hot new place every week, and sometimes the cadence of openings—as well as rising chefs, new concepts, and freshly renovated rooms—can make your head spin. Of course, there are always the old haunts, the standbys—but isn’t it fun to have some new players on the scene?

There are plenty of fresh restaurants this fall, so if you’re looking for the best and buzziest new restaurants to add to your list, Vogue has you covered. For this list, we focused on places that opened in the past three months. There’s the trio of Bangkok women bringing heartwarming Thai food to a homey West Village space, an Afro-Caribbean brasserie and bakery from an award-winning chef, a beloved South Indian pop-up turned brick-and-mortar gem, and more.

Below, read our picks for the best new restaurants in New York City.

Tucked along the westernmost stretch of Christopher Street, this new Afro-Caribbean bakery and brasserie is making everyone’s mornings a bit cheerier with its sorghum banana bread and beef patty croissants. Calabash opened its doors in early October and is Chef Camari Mick’s first solo restaurant following her role as executive pastry chef of the Musket Room and Raf’s. (She opened alongside chef de cuisine Tajeh Porter.) Daytime service is great for grabbing laminated pastries and breakfast sandwiches from the case, but if you have time to sit down, the fluffy cornbread pancakes drizzled with salted maple sabayon just might ruin all future pancakes for you.

And if you’re really ready to commit (trust me, you are), they’re also offering a five-course prix fixe served Friday and Saturday evenings, with one seating at 6:30 p.m. Dishes like Hoppin’ John Dolma wrapped in collard greens, and red snapper with sweet corn and étouffée-style gravy explore the connections between the diaspora and classical techniques, and are paired with house-fermented mocktails. The restaurant is named for the vessel that has traveled across the African diaspora throughout history, and Chef Mick’s menu highlights traditions found across West Africa, the Caribbean, and America’s Eastern seaboard. As if all of that wasn't worth firing up your OpenTable, I’ve yet to mention the interiors. The 30-seat, 1,300-square-foot space was designed by D.C.-based Drummond Projects (very cozy, very refined), and they also partnered with gallerist Cierra Britton on an exhibition of paintings by BIPOC women artists. —Nicole Kliest, contributing writer

Turn the corner onto East Broadway, past the bustling crowds of Bar Oliver, and you’ll find Cavalier, a Mediterranean-inspired restaurant and wine bar from Chef Mason Lindahl, Tate Jackson, and Yasmin Kaytmaz (who also owns The River). They’ve got pink tables, black leather booths, low lighting, and a private dining room in the back with a dreamlike mural by Georgia Gardner Gray.

The vibe at Cavalier is friendly and earnest, a welcome contrast to the sometimes aloof, cooler-than-thou energy of some of the other nearby see-and-be-seen spots. But the real star here is Chef Lindahl’s food, which feels fancy and comforting all at once. You’ll want to get at least one order of the baked lavash bread, which is served with tomato butter and eggplant, and is so warm and soft you could curl up and take a nap in it.

I also loved the chicken liver mousse, the tender and flavorful duck, and the chocolate mousse for dessert. Double mousse, yes: If it seems decadent, it is, but somehow you leave feeling lighter. They also have what my wine friends call a “serious” wine list, with extensive bottle offerings and fun by-the-glass options, including a red blend from Château Musar, the cult-favorite Lebanese producer. —Anna Grace Lee, lifestyle writer

The vibes might be pleasantly low-key at this new Mexican seafood spot in the West Village, but the food and wine are worth planning an entire evening around. El Camarón Peludo opened this past September on Cornelia Street (next door to the now shuttered Pearl Oyster Bar) and was conceived by the team behind Taqueria Ramirez and Carnitas Ramírez, Giovanni Cervantes and Tania Apolinar, as well as Mexico City-born chef Carlos Barrera. The restaurant is walk-in only, and feels like the love child of a Spanish tapas bar and a quintessential Mexican kitchen.

By their own admission, the menu is an unapologetic celebration of shrimp (all hail the cute crustacean!). Order them raw, chilled, grilled, boiled, or otherwise, and your taste buds are in for a ride. In fact, there’s even a shrimp-shaped lantern hanging above the raw bar, if you appreciate commitment to a theme. Complement all that freshness with their salsa, like the one made from four different chiles, and a wine selection that will knock your socks off. —N.K.

Straker’s is an exercise in controlled chaos. The first New York outpost from Thomas Straker, the TikTok-famous British chef known for his namesake Notting Hill restaurant and “bad boy” reputation, Straker’s is a place where the room is loud, the bouncer wears leather, and the food is excellent.

When I went on a Tuesday a few weeks after opening, the room seemed full of vaguely businessy men and models, everyone’s faces blurring in candlelight, the glow interrupted by the flash of phones eating first. Is this the place to come for a long overdue catch-up with a friend, or a first date? No. I want to come here with three friends and sit in the corner sipping martinis while the loud, untz-untz music bass-shakes the banquettes and drowns out our gossip.

I could easily eat two of the wood-fired mussel flatbread, which is like pizza crust dipped in buttery mussel sauce. The duck was tender, the potatoes perfectly crispy. Dessert is also important. The rainbow array of ice creams is sure to spark debate (we went with the burnt honey, which was nice and not too sweet), but no matter what you do, get the chocolate tart. Don’t skip the cucumber salad either, which offered a pleasingly fresh crunch to balance out the indulgence—though indulgence is the name of the game here. That is, of course, if you can get a reservation. —A.G.L.

Adding to the city’s dynamic supper club scene, chef Lana Lagomarsini opened Creola on the Upper East Side this past September, following her time as chef de cuisine at Francis Mallmann’s Garzón in Uruguay, as well as cooking stints at Gramercy Tavern, Daniel, and Momofuku Ko. The opening menu kicked off with flavors like elk with blackberry jerk and plantain, and an oxtail pâté en croûte (evoking a Jamaican beef patty). The wines are sourced from low-intervention producers from France and Spain, and can either be paired with each course or purchased by the glass or bottle. (Top points for the fact that every bottle is priced under $100!) Fortify your appetite for dessert, which at the moment is a sassafras flan crowned with a poached cherry and bay leaf oil.

The restaurant’s name is a sentimental homage to Lagomarsini’s grandmother, Creola, who lived on the Upper West Side and crossed Central Park every afternoon to pick her up from school, located just five blocks from where the restaurant now stands. There’s even a framed photo of her grandmother that hangs in the dining room, which makes the experience feel all the more intimate and homey. Speaking of the interiors, the design was impressively handled by Lagomarsini herself, who sourced antique furniture and hemmed the curtains by hand. Creola has 12 seats and is open Wednesday through Saturday beginning at 5 p.m. with two seatings a night. —N.K.

When I heard that the Portuguese chef Nuno Sousa—of Leitão in the West Village, where I’ve enjoyed tapas and not-too-sweet margaritas—was opening a new restaurant nearby on West 10th Street, I was curious to try it. Galo, which is in a historic 1860s carriage house, is a warm space decorated with ceramic art where you can have suckling pig, octopus that slices as smooth as butter, and tender picanha. They have an extensive Portuguese wine list, but I loved the Só mais uma cocktail (a refreshing mojito-like mix of gin, matcha, mint, lime, and Portuguese herbal liqueur), and the potato pavé, which was crispy and crunchy like thin slices of potato paper. —A.G.L.

Hommali is the debut restaurant from a team of three Thai women—chef Chattchakorn “Benz” Khajornchaisan, general manager Kritayanee “Air” Promsarin and operations lead Pichalak “Picha” Srigungvarl—all Bangkok natives who became friends while working in the New York City restaurant scene. They’ve put a lot of hometown heart into Hommali, which takes its name from hom mali, which is Thai for “fragrant jasmine rice.”

You can feel the camaraderie in the air of the cozy West Village space. Paintings from Bangkok’s Chatuchak Weekend Market line the walls of the den-like downstairs dining room, and dishes like tom yum seafood cocktail are served in a beautiful shell. I loved the Panang curry beef cheek and the five-spice duck with duck fat rice, plus the passionfruit cocktail with a bubble-bath-like topping, and delicious toasted rice ice cream with coconut for dessert. —A.G.L.

Over the past few years, Top Chef alum Rasika Venkatesa has built up a devoted following with her Mythily pop-ups. Now, Chef Venkatesa’s progressive South Indian restaurant has found a brick-and-mortar home in Williamsburg. Named in honor of Venkatesa’s grandmother, the restaurant draws on her childhood in Chennai, techniques she learned while traveling across Tamil Nadu, and her fine-dining training at The French Laundry and Mourad.

When I went for dinner not long after its opening in late September, every table was full. People craned their necks to look at the vibrant, artful dishes landing on each table. I got my spoon out to scoop up all the delicious, creamy sauce of the Lamb Sukka Dumplings, which is a must-order, along with the Benne Dosa, the chicken, and the confit potato roast with sambar béarnaise, plus the “filter coffee soft-serve.” —A.G.L.

Some of my most memorable meals have been in Brazil (first time ant consumption, for example), and while I don’t have immediate travel plans to return to the South American culinary capital, thankfully, I have Iara. Chef Vitor Mendes’s new restaurant in the Lower East Side takes inspiration from the Amazon Rainforest and is named for the region’s water goddess. The 60-seat, open-kitchen concept was designed by New York-based practice Studio WDM and channels the Amazon’s soil for its painterly color palette (swirls of chocolate brown, burnt oranges, and terracotta dance across the walls and tables).

Menu-wise, it’s basically a who’s who of Amazonian heavyweight flavors: tapioca crisps gilded with smoked trout mousse and biquinho pepper, cheese bread with smoked eggplant dip, Brazilian red snapper stew with red palm dendê oil, tucupi, and coconut milk. If you’re looking to impress your dining mate, go for the charcoal-grilled tambaqui, a large Amazonian river fish that the team brushes with a spice blend and serves alongside stewed butter beans, tapioca fries, and açaí ketchup. —N.K.

These days, the word “sexy” is thrown around a lot when describing a restaurant, but 148 Noble actually is sexy. The French and New Orleans-inspired bistro, on a quiet residential street in Greenpoint, is candlelit and cozy. It’s small, but not too small. The service is attentive, with a slightly conspiratorial air that makes you feel like you’re all in on the same secret. A misstep is corrected by a heavier-than-usual wine pour. Yes, the portions might be a bit small, but every bite is flavorful. The chef, Gabriel Borges, is from New Orleans and used to work at Chez Ma Tante down the street. Bring your date and get the pommes paillasson (a Jenga tower of fancy French fries, basically), the duck with honeynut squash and pickled ají dulce, and the rich chocolate tarte with crème fraîche. —A.G.L.

Why have a normal-portioned meal when an all-you-can-eat buffet is an option? It’s a fair question to ask yourself prior to arriving at Good Time Country Buffet, which translates a cherished Southern dining tradition to the East Village. This is the third restaurant from Good Time Hospitality, the same team behind Kisa and C as in Charlie. If you’ve been to either of the aforementioned hotspots, you’re already aware the team was born in Korea and raised in Atlanta, with both of these distinct culinary identities cleverly finding their way onto the menus.

For this concept, they turned to the classic buffets they grew up going to, and programmed the menu to be a fixed-price, self-serve extravaganza. Fried chicken, collard greens, cornbread, mac and cheese, ice cream sundaes—the sky’s the limit, friends. And as far as inspiration goes, they didn’t stop at the menus. The interiors were designed by Two Point Zero and echo classic country buffets with wood paneling, patterned wallpapers, and—rather thoughtfully—carpeted floors, which traditionally have been used to ensure seniors don’t slip and fall while getting their buffet on. (Seniors coming to Good Time Country Buffet also receive a discounted price.) This opening especially strikes a chord with co-owner David Yun, who, as a kid, joined produce delivery routes to Georgia country buffets with his father, who still works in the same role. As part of the restaurant’s research and development process, Yun rejoined his father on those routes. —N.K.

Humm, Daniel Humm’s first namesake restaurant, is about as buzzy as it gets. The cavernous 7,731-square-foot space—which was home to EN Japanese Brasserie for 20 years—has been transformed by Humm and interior designer Pierre Yovanovitch, along with artists Francesco Clemente and Rashid Johnson. The room glows with light from taper candles encased in glass on each table. A sunset tile mural frames the 16-foot wood-fired hearth oven, and it all feels a little like being in another world for the night. Everyone gets the caviar bagel, which is good (it’s a miniature bagel with caviar, after all), but my favorite dishes were the tomato focaccia and the milk and honey soft-serve sundae. —A.G.L.

In a sea of nostalgic-themed restaurants, Booth’s Extra Fine should go to the top of your must-try list. It’s not a club masquerading as a steakhouse; it’s the real deal. Chef Nick Pfannerstill, who worked at the now-closed Michelin-starred restaurant Dovetail and is co-owner of the cocktail bar Nobody Told Me, is serving smoky steaks that cast a pleasant aroma over the room, cold and balanced martinis, a butter roll that glistens, Caesar salad with garlic bread-like croutons, shrimp voodoo. Everything I had was delicious, and it was fun to try various sauces on offer, including salsa verde and aged brandy peppercorn. For dessert, get the bourbon chocolate cake, which may fulfill my years-long search for a chocolate cake as decadent as the one in Matilda. —A.G.L.

#6600. Cream Cheese Mashed Potatoes

Cream cheese doesn't just belong on bagels. In this instance, it's the secret to making mashed potatoes even creamier, richer, and more decadent. The high fat content in the cream cheese melds with the butter and milk to make the potatoes perfectly fluffy and creamy. Serve these at your Thanksgiving or Christmas dinner, or even on a cozy weeknight alongside oven-baked pork chops.

What People Are Saying:“Never cooked mashed potatoes before, and this recipe turned out amazing.” - GreenHat

“Silky smooth and delicious” - BlueProcessor

In a large pot, cover the potatoes with water and season with salt. Bring it to a boil and cook until the potatoes are softened and fork-tender, which should take about 16 to 18 minutes. Drain and return the potatoes to the pot.

Add cream cheese and, using a potato masher, mash potatoes until smooth.

Meanwhile, in a small saucepan over medium heat, cook the milk and butter. Stir until the butter is melted, which should take about 2 minutes. Pour the butter mixture over the potatoes.

Stir until it's combined and creamy. Make sure to season with salt and pepper!

Transfer potatoes to a serving bowl and season with more pepper. Top with chives and enjoy!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover cream cheese mashed potatoes in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days.

#6599. Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly’s Full Relationship Timeline

Dakota Johnson and Machine Gun Kelly have yet to define their relationship publicly, but the two stars have been spending plenty of time together.

The actress and musician were first linked in September 2026, when they were photographed together in New York City. Days later, a source told People that Johnson and Kelly, whose real name is Colson Baker, “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The two stars had known each other before, but according to the source, they became closer after attending Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in July.

Since then, Johnson has watched Kelly walk the runway in Milan, and sources have shared more about how their connection developed.

Below, everything we know about Johnson and Kelly’s rumored relationship so far.

Johnson and Kelly both attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

The two stars already knew each other, but a source close to Kelly told People in September that they “hit it off” at the wedding.

On September 28, a source gave Entertainment Tonight similar intel, telling the outlet that Johnson and Kelly “really connected at Taylor and Travis’s wedding.”

On September 12, Johnson and Kelly were photographed together in New York City, getting out of the same SUV and entering Swift’s Tribeca apartment.

Four days later, a source close to Kelly told People that Kelly and Johnson “have been hanging out and seeing each other under the radar for months now.”

The source explained that Johnson and Kelly “started off as friends and were texting often, but now they’re spending more time together.”

“It’s a very new start, but they’re smitten with each other right now,” the insider added. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet. They are just seeing where spending time together will take them.”

A second source characterized things as “super casual” at that point.

On September 22, Johnson and Kelly both traveled to Italy for Milan Fashion Week and attended the same event.

Three days later, Johnson addressed the broader attention her dating life receives during an appearance on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, though she never mentioned Kelly specifically.

“Even if I go to dinner with my manager or my lawyer, it’s like, ‘Seen with mystery man,’” she said. “I also don’t care.”

When asked whether she ever feels compelled to correct speculation about her personal life, Johnson explained why she prefers not to engage with it.

“I think it’s just futile. People are gonna believe what they wanna believe, and I don’t have the energy to fight for that,” she said. “I would much rather focus on other things in my life. Every day, there’s something on the internet that’s ridiculous and true or not true, and I don’t care.”

On September 28, a source shared more about Kelly and Johnson’s relationship with Entertainment Tonight: “Dakota was the one who made the first move. He’s very shy around her, but he likes her a lot. It’s still new, but they’re having fun and seeing where things go.”

The insider added, “Dakota has been a fan of his music and has always found him cute. He likes her a lot, too.”

On October 19, a source close to Kelly told People that he and Johnson were spending more time together. “They have been out on dates that people don’t know about because there aren’t any photos.”

The insider said that they’re in the “dating phase,” and “aren’t ready to go official yet.”

“They both really like each other and have been seeing each other more frequently,” the source shared. “They haven’t put a label on their relationship yet, but they’re growing closer every time they hang out.”

In the past few months, they’ve especially connected over their “same dry and dark sense of humor,” the source said. “[They] make each other laugh.”

Days later, Kelly and Johnson were photographed out in Los Angeles on October 23. They first left a music studio together, riding off in Kelly’s red Maserati. That evening, they were seen together again, leaving the Chateau Marmont.

A source close to Johnson gave People an update on their dynamic on October 28. “She’s happy and enjoys spending time with him,” the insider said. “There’s a lot of chemistry and she’s been going to the studio with him while he works. For now, it makes her happy.”

On November 3, Kelly and Johnson were photographed leaving a restaurant in Calabasas, California, after a dinner date. They were smiling and talking to each other in the shots.

Two days later, on November 5, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles, attending a Khaite dinner at Dan Tana’s in West Hollywood. For the occasion, Johnson wore a black Death Row Pictures zip-up hoodie over a lace-trimmed Valentino miniskirt, paired with knee-high Gucci boots and statement diamond jewelry. Kelly opted for a more casual look, wearing a green satin bomber jacket over a yellow hoodie and gray sweatpants.

The next week, Johnson and Kelly stepped out for another evening together in Los Angeles on November 11. #6598. Cider-Braised Sausage and Lentils

I haven’t made a meal in the French countryside in fall; but sometimes I dream, and these slow-cooked lentils are what I’d make in such a situation. Back in my American reality, it still makes an excellent dinner or hearty weekend lunch. Look for mild smoked Austrian or German sausages, which lean on mellow herbs and warm spices (sometimes, if you’re lucky, they’re also stuffed with a nutty cheese)—this style is already cooked to a safe temperature, but the casing’s texture is greatly improved when seared before reheating. If your shop only carries sweet Italian sausage or something like an apple-stuffed chicken sausage, both work in a pinch. What a treat it will be to actually finish off that gallon of apple cider you impulsively bought last week in the lentil-braising liquid.

More great fall recipes this way: Charred Cabbage With Sausages and Apples; Pork Chops With Green Chiles and Apples; Mustardy Cider-Braised Pork Chops.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or a medium heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 6–8 smoked Austrian or German sausages (1–1½ lb.), turning often, until deeply browned on all sides, about 4 minutes. Transfer to a plate.

Combine 1 large red or yellow onion, finely chopped, 3 celery stalks, finely chopped, 1 large carrot, peeled, finely chopped, 1 tsp. freshly ground pepper, and ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in same pan. Reduce heat to medium and cook, stirring often and scraping up any browned bits stuck to bottom of pan, until vegetables are softened, 6–8 minutes. Add 5 garlic cloves, thinly sliced, and cook, stirring, just until fragrant, about 1 minute.

Add 2 cups low-sodium chicken or vegetable broth, 1½ cups apple cider, 1½ cups French green lentils, picked through, rinsed, ½ cup finely chopped parsley, 3 Tbsp. Dijon or whole grain mustard, and remaining ½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt to pan. Increase heat to high and bring to a boil. Cook until liquid is slightly reduced, about 5 minutes. Cover pan, reduce heat to medium-low, and cook until lentils are tender and most of the liquid is absorbed but mixture is still saucy, 30–35 minutes.

Uncover pan and stir in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar or red wine vinegar. Nestle sausages into lentil mixture and add any juices pooled on plate. Simmer until sausages are warmed through, about 5 minutes. Top with parsley leaves and reserved celery leaves to serve.

#6594. Broiled Salmon Teriyaki

Sometimes all it takes to make dinner feel special is a big, bold piece of protein. Case in point: This salty-sweet salmon glazed in a glossy teriyaki-style sauce. Brushed in two rounds with the quick sauce made with nothing more than sugar, soy sauce, sesame oil, and vinegar, the salmon sizzles under the broiler, charring as it takes on a smoky flavor. This recipe calls for one large piece of salmon, but you can use smaller fillets or opt for a white fish such as cod or halibut. Just note that the cooking time will be shorter if using smaller pieces, so keep an eye on them. Add a quick garnish of sliced scallions and toasted sesame seeds, and dinner is done.

More salmon winners this way: Hot Honey-Glazed Salmon; Green Curry-Glazed Salmon; and Slow-Roasted Salmon With Harissa.

Bring ⅓ cup (packed; 67 g) dark brown sugar, ¼ cup soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. unseasoned rice vinegar, and 2 tsp. toasted sesame oil to a simmer in a small saucepan over medium-high heat; cook until reduced by half and syrupy, 5–7 minutes. Let sauce cool until thickened slightly, about 10 minutes.

Heat broiler (if broiler is in your oven, place rack in upper third). Season both sides of one 1½–2-lb. skinless or skin-on center-cut salmon fillet with kosher salt. Place, skin side down, in a skillet or baking dish. Transfer one third of sauce to a small bowl and set aside for serving. Brush about half of remaining sauce over fillet. (If the salmon has a lot of room around it in the pan, line with foil to prevent runoff sauce from burning onto pan.)

Broil salmon until sauce is just starting to burn in spots, 4–7 minutes. Brush remaining sauce over fillet and broil until deeply charred and salmon is opaque all the way through, about 5 minutes.

Remove fish from oven and spoon reserved sauce over. Top with thinly sliced scallions and/or toasted sesame seeds if desired.

#6592. I’ve Finally Found Sunscreens for Oily Skin That Actually Stay Shine-Free

As a beauty editor, sunscreen is a near-daily topic of conversation, practically as commonplace as the weather. But when you have oily skin, finding the right formula isn’t about picking up the next new tube, but finding one that won’t slide off my face; or even worse, one that yields a breakout. Sometimes it feels like I can either protect my skin from UV rays or create a whole new set of skin problems.

Sunscreen remains one of the trickiest skin-care categories to get right when you have oily skin. You want something that protects your skin without feeling greasy, clogging pores, or pilling under makeup; a balance that board-certified dermatologist Marnie Nussbaum, MD knows all too well. “I always tell my patients that oily skin still needs hydration and daily sun protection, but I often get pushback because sunscreens can feel heavy or leave behind a greasy finish for those with oily skin.”

Thankfully, there’s no shortage of options these days, from mineral and chemical filters to tinted and shockingly clear formulas, with finishes ranging from matte to luminous. There’s also an entire world of SPF out there, and I send an eye emoji every time I hear a friend is headed to Paris, Seoul, Tokyo, or Sydney. They know exactly what I’m after.

After plenty of trial and error, I’ve learned to pay close attention to whether a formula is noncomedogenic, meaning it’s designed not to clog pores. I even run ingredient lists through online acne checkers for good measure. Board-certified dermatologist Shereen Teymour, MD, recommends looking for not just non-comedogenic formulas, but ingredients like niacinamide, glycerin, or hyaluronic acid, which can help balance oil production and support the skin barrier without contributing to a greasy feel. “One of the biggest misconceptions is that oily skin does not need hydration,” she explains. “In reality, dehydrated skin can sometimes compensate by producing even more oil.”

Ultimately, the best sunscreens for oily skin offer lightweight textures and comfortable finishes that make you actually want to apply them every day. Below, the formulas I’d recommend, plus how to apply them so you’re glowing, not glistening—and always protected from the sun.

What to Look for in a Sunscreen for Oily Skin

For those with oily skin, board-certified dermatologist Dara Spearman, MD, says the number one thing to look for is a noncomedogenic formula. Dr. Brendan Camp, MD, a double-board-certified dermatologist and dermatopathologist, adds that oil-free, lightweight sunscreens with a mattifying or gel-based texture tend to work best. “A gel-based formula may work better than a heavy cream,” says Spearman. “Some brands even offer liquid sunscreens that dry down to a matte finish, which is ideal for oily skin.”

Should oily skin types use mineral or chemical sunscreens?

It really just depends on your preference. “Oily skin types can use mineral or chemical sunscreens but should look for a lightweight, noncomedogenic formula,” says Camp. However, Spearman suggests opting for mineral formulas, noting that “chemical-based sunscreens can leave skin feeling greasy.”

Can I skip moisturizer and use sunscreen for oily skin?

While it’s always best to experiment and see what works for your skin, Spearman says it’s absolutely fine to skip moisturizer if you’re using a sunscreen that suits your needs. “Doubling up with moisturizer and sunscreen is not necessary for those with oily skin. In fact, I often recommend that my acne-prone patients skip moisturizer in the morning and instead use their medications followed by sunscreen,” she explains. Camp adds that if you do opt to skip moisturizer, make sure your sunscreen offers added skin benefits beyond UV protection. “This might include hydration, skin-barrier support, and antioxidant protection,” he says.

Why does my sunscreen make my face so oily?

“Many sunscreens are composed of emollients or oils to help moisturize the skin and improve spreadability,” Spearman explains. “This can make facial skin, which naturally has more oil glands, appear even oilier.” She also notes that some barrier sunscreens can trap sebum or natural oils on the skin’s surface, which contributes to a greasy look. Camp adds that products made with emollient or occlusive ingredients are more likely to trap oil, while lightweight liquid or gel-based sunscreens tend to leave a more matte finish.

How to Wear Sunscreen Without Looking Greasy

If greasiness is one of your main concerns, look for a matte-based physical sunscreen in either a liquid or gel formula or one with a naturally mattifying finish. Camp recommends ingredients like niacinamide, silica, and zinc—all of which may help reduce shine. Another option, according to Spearman, is to skip moisturizer altogether and consider using a powder-based sunscreen for reapplication throughout the day.

First, we lean on Vogue’s vast network of experts—from board-certified dermatologists to celebrity aestheticians—to gain professional acumen on the industry’s standout products, ones these specialists would actually use on their clients. We pair their expertise with our editorial best practices to curate the thoughtful edits you read on our site.

As it relates to sunscreens for oily skin, we selected the best based on the following characteristics: ingredients, texture, finish, SPF level, UV filters, broad-spectrum coverage, and the skin-care concerns they address. #6590. 10 Airbnbs in Sweden for a Stylish Winter Getaway

For all the lakeside escapades and long, light-filled days of Scandi summer, something about winter in Sweden feels especially apropos. True, the sun is basically a missing person until April; but between the Christmas markets, the reindeer running loose in the northern part of the country, the sauna traditions, and the copious amounts of glögg being poured at cafés, it’s about as cozy and festive as it gets. (Provided, of course, you pack the right layers.)

Experience all this up close is by booking an Airbnb; whether it’s an apartment on the outskirts of Stockholm or a quiet escape that’s significantly more remote, a home of your own is the best way to truly get a feel for this special time of year.

Try an 18th-century cottage surrounded by fields and wetlands for brisk winter walks; or perhaps a colorful jewel box apartment right in Stockholm (complete with a terrace, if you’re willing to brave the cold for your morning coffee). We even found a cabin on your very own personal island; if you want to go truly off the grid, WiFi-free and everything, it’s the vacation rental for you.

Keep reading for our favorite Airbnbs in Sweden to book this winter.

Located in Midsommarkransen, a residential neighborhood dotted with boutiques and cafés, this bright studio does color well. From pine-green limewash in the bedroom to terracotta-colored windows, it’s the antidote to winter blues—it even has a large balcony. (Admittedly, a less-tempting amenity in the winter months; but if you’re feeling brave enough to take your mug of glögg al fresco, the twinkle lights set a cozy scene.)

Known for its farm shops selling local delicacies and small fishing villages, Österlen is a great option for your Swedish trip. Set the scene for your stay with this cozy home. It dates back to 1901, with soaring ceilings and whitewashed wood panels that make it feel even more spacious than it is. It comes with four bikes you can use for the duration of your stay—in more temperate months, cycle out to one of the aforementioned farm stands for dinner ingredients.

This two-bedroom home is waterfront living at its finest. Designed by an architecture, it sits on the contemporary side with brutalist-like concrete walls and floor-to-ceiling windows. Rent a car to explore the archipelago—you’ll be near both Stockholm and the beaches for day trips.

Amenities: Washer, TV, grill, outdoor dining, pool, free parking

The coastal town of Landskrona has a lot to offer, not least of all this unique property. Antique furnishings and high ceilings give it a stately feel, with plenty of decor ideas to bookmark—starting with the lace canopy curtains in the bedroom. Want to bring back a piece of your holiday? All the furniture in the apartment is actually for sale; inquire within to purchase.

#6589. Chili Crisp Yogurt Chicken

Slather Greek yogurt and your favorite chili crisp on chicken thighs, roast in a hot oven, and you’ll be rewarded with juicy, tender meat with a delightful orange-tinged exterior. But the best part of this sheet-pan dinner comes after the chicken is cooked: Spread cooked rice into the pan’s juices, then slide the baking sheet back into the oven. As the rice soaks up the deeply savory sauce, it will crisp in spots, creating a texture that’s somewhere between chewy-fluffy steamed grains and a freshly toasted pita chip. And when it comes to chili crisp, we love the iconic and easy-to-source Lao Gan Ma, but specialty brands like Fly By Jing are great too—just make sure the one you use is not too spicy, which will overpower the dish.

More great chicken and rice recipes this way: One-Pot Chicken Thighs With Cilantro Rice and Beans; Spiced Coconut Chicken Rice; Nana’s Chicken and Rice Stew.

Preheat oven to 425°. Season 6–8 skinless, boneless chicken thighs (1½–2 lb.) with 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt.

Whisk together ¾ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt and ¼ cup plus 2 Tbsp. well-stirred chili crisp in a large bowl. Add chicken thighs and toss to coat.

Arrange chicken on a rimmed baking sheet and top with any yogurt mixture left in bowl. Bake chicken until deeply browned and an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part of a thigh registers 165°, 25–30 minutes. Transfer chicken to a cutting board or plate.

Spread 3 cups cooked jasmine or short-grain rice over baking sheet with chicken juices and bake until most of the juices have been absorbed and rice is starting to crisp in spots, 12–15 minutes.

Meanwhile, whisk together 1 Tbsp. finely grated lime zest, ¼ cup fresh lime juice, ½ tsp. sugar, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, and remaining ¼ cup plain whole-milk Greek yogurt in a small bowl.

Combine ½ medium head of green cabbage (about 1 lb.), very thinly sliced, and a big pinch of Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt in a large bowl. Using your hands, scrunch cabbage gently to soften. Add 1 small red onion, thinly sliced, 1 cup finely chopped cilantro, and yogurt dressing and toss to combine. Taste cabbage slaw and season with more salt if needed.

Slice chicken as desired and serve with crisped rice and cabbage slaw.

#6588. Turkey Cheese Ball

The turkey may be the main event of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can be a snack, too! Whether you're hosting Thanksgiving for your community or celebrating with family, this fun appetizer is the perfect way to get everyone excited for the big turkey dinner with another smaller turkey! This cheese ball is not only the most eye-catching appetizer you can add to your holiday menu, but it’s surprisingly easy to create.

What People Are Saying:“I made this for Friendsgiving. It was delicious and I got several comments on how great it tasted.” - kellykcox34580

In a food processor, pulse the cream cheese, goat cheese, butter, and garlic powder until the mixture is smooth. Add parsley, chives, and thyme and pulse until well combined. Then season with salt and black pepper.

Transfer the cream cheese mixture to a piece of plastic wrap and gather up the wrap to form a ball. Then transfer the mixture into a large bowl and refrigerate until it’s firm, which should take at least three hours and up to one day.

In a clean food processor, pulse 3/4 cup pecan halves until they are finely chopped.

Roll the cheese ball in nuts and arrange it all on a platter.

Start by cutting a large triangle from a red bell pepper—this will be the face. Next, cut a smaller triangle from a yellow bell pepper for the beak. For the eyes, slice two small rounds from a small carrot. Take a larger carrot and slice it into diagonal ovals to make the feet, then carve little triangles at one end to look like toes. Finally, thinly slice the rest of the carrots into matchsticks for the tail.

Grab some toothpicks and stick the carrot eyes onto the red triangle face. Then, use another toothpick to add the yellow beak to the face—just make sure all the toothpicks point toward the back so you can attach everything to the cheese ball later. Now, press the face onto the front of the cheese ball, and slide the carrot feet into the base.

Insert matchstick carrots, pretzel sticks, and mini pretzels into the back of the ball to create the tail. Using the remaining 1/2 cup pecan halves, create wings by overlapping them along each side of the ball. Serve with crackers alongside!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Store leftover cheese ball in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 4 days. If possible, remove the pretzels and vegetable decorations before storing, as they can soften over time.

#6585. Soothing Rice Porridge

This is a Japanese-style rice porridge known as okayu. I ate this every morning in the early weeks of postpartum after my first daughter was born. It’s what our family reaches for whenever we need a simple, nourishing dish that warms from the inside out. For the smoothest porridge, let the rice soak in cold water before cooking.

If you have time, soak the rice, which makes the texture softer and can aid in digestion. Place washed rice in a bowl and pour in water to cover by 1". Soak at least 30 minutes and up to 4 hours. Drain off excess water before starting the recipe. The wakame seaweed, which you’ve probably had in miso soup, can typically be found dried anywhere Asian groceries are available.

In The Fourth Trimester, we ask parents: What meal nourished you after welcoming your baby? This month it’s a cozy rice porridge by Eating at Home cookbook author Trinity Mouzon Wofford. Read more: Breakfast at Home, After Birth at Home.

Combine 1 cup short-grain rice, washed, soaked if desired, ¼ cup dried wakame (seaweed), 1 Tbsp. dried red shiso, and 6 cups low-sodium broth (any kind) or water in a large donabe, medium Dutch oven, or other heavy pot. Cover and bring to a boil over medium-high heat (you’ll hear bubbling). Uncover and stir, making sure nothing is stuck to bottom of pot. Cover and reduce heat to low. Continue to cook porridge 30 minutes more (resist the urge to peek).

Remove pot from heat and let porridge sit (still covered) 10 minutes. Uncover and stir. Rice grains should be cooked through, broken open, and creamy, but porridge should still be fairly loose. Season porridge with fine sea salt.

Ladle porridge into bowls and serve, topped with toasted sesame seeds, toasted sesame oil, and/or thinly sliced scallions.

#6584. Poulet Basquaise

Rich tomatoes, stewed onions and peppers, and tender bone-in chicken make this Spanish- and French-inspired poulet Basquaise recipe extremely flavorful while still being surprisingly easy to make. Savory and rustic, it’s a stew that’s ideal for making ahead and enjoying all week long. The key ingredient? Piment d’Espelette—the regional spice known for its peppery, smoky essence. If you’re looking to master a classic dish or simply want a reliable, cozy weeknight dinner, then this recipe won’t let you down.

Heat a large skillet with oil and season the chicken with salt. Working in batches, add the chicken pieces and sear until the skin is golden in color, which should take 5 to 7 minutes. Remove the chicken to a heatproof plate.

Then reduce the heat and add the onion, bell peppers, garlic, piment d’Espelette, and salt. You’ll want to stir this once in a while so it doesn’t stick, but also let the vegetables soften. This should take 8 to 10 minutes.

At this point, increase the heat again and add the wine. Scrape up any bits on the bottom and allow those peppers and onions to absorb the wine. The liquid should reduce.

Add the tomatoes and broth and bring to a simmer. Be careful of splattering sauce and adjust the heat as needed. Place the chicken back into the skillet, skin side up, and cook until the chicken is tender and nearly falling off the bone. The sauce should also be thicker and fragrant. This should take about 30 to 40 minutes.

Stir in the chorizo and cook until it’s warmed through. Top it off with thyme and serve!

The full list of ingredients and instructions can be found in the recipe below.

Let cool and store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. It’s certainly a great meal-prep dish. Make this on a Sunday night for lunch Monday and Tuesday.
