#6547. E.T., Phone Chanel! How Fashion’s Labels Got Personal Again

E.T., phone home! Or if you’re Steven Spielberg getting honored at the Museum of Modern Art’s annual Film Benefit, phone Chanel. On Thursday night, Spielberg offered a peek inside his bespoke Chanel tuxedo jacket, courtesy of Matthieu Blazy. Beneath the classic black tailoring was a galaxy-speckled lining, an embroidered playing card featuring E.T. on his bicycle, and a little patch reading “E.T. PHONE HOME.” Spielberg proudly flashed the details for all to see. Now that’s a statement lining.

It’s just the latest in a series of delightfully personal flourishes coming out of Blazy’s Chanel atelier. For his spring 2026 haute couture debut, the designer asked models to contribute something meaningful to their looks: a love letter, a birth date, a lucky symbol, an intimate thought. These were translated into exquisite embroideries by the house’s Lesage atelier, stitched into garments or onto little silk notes tucked inside delicate, translucent Chanel handbags. Model Stephanie Cavalli reportedly chose a letter from her husband. The sentiment was just as beautiful as the craftsmanship.

Blazy has continued to play with this notion of garments carrying memories. In the lead up to the spring 2027 Chanel show, models Bhavitha Mandava and Awar Odhiang discovered embroidered playing cards tucked inside jacket linings, depicting Gabrielle Chanel wearing looks the models themselves had previously walked down the runway in.

Couture clients can reportedly request this kind of personalization, too. And at October’s Academy Museum Gala, meanwhile, Hailey Bieber’s custom bubblegum-pink Chanel gown concealed another tender, handwritten detail: a note that featured the name of her son, Jack, accompanied by an arrow-pierced heart.

Leaving something deeply personal inside a garment is hardly new. Alexander McQueen famously made a rebellious art of it. While working for Romeo Gigli in Milan, the young designer reportedly left a rather less romantic message inside a jacket after being made to repeatedly redo its construction: “Fuck you, Romeo.” There are also the legendary tales—though disputed—of profanities hidden inside suits made for Prince Charles during his Savile Row apprenticeship. More poignantly, McQueen stitched locks of his own hair into the linings of his 1992 graduate collection, Jack the Ripper Stalks His Victims, and later used them in his clothing labels.

But the clothing label itself has also long been a place for designers to express a little personality. Spend an afternoon rifling through the racks of any good thrift store and you’ll find a rag-tag assortment of embroidered crests, elaborate cursive fonts, wacky illustrations, and wonderfully earnest mottos from long-forgotten local dressmakers to grand houses. Even Burberry’s evolving labels offer a miniature history of the brand: from the old Burberrys name and the original Equestrian Knight emblem, introduced in 1901, to the pared-back modernist identity of recent years, and Daniel Lee’s revival of the knight in 2023. A label can do so, so much more than simply announce who made something.

A new generation of designers is rediscovering the joy of these small, characterful details. Take Sofia Testino, whose young eponymous label imagines a whole world of professions and their fictional, more off-kilter wardrobes. It’s been a joy to watch her brand identity develop through old-fashioned woven labels, with evolving colorful geometric borders, winged crests, and the tagline: “Style, Quality, Value.” There are shoeboxes bearing a cartoonish evolution from ape to woman in high heels. Testino has spoken about collecting vintage labels and old flight-attendant uniforms, mixing and matching elements to create her own distinctive identity. “I feel like labels and packaging and all these little details have been lost,” she recently told Welcome.jpeg. Where so many brands have settled for homogenizing, identity-flattening minimalism, she’s building an entire universe (and its fleet of well-dressed staff) down to the last stitch.

Elsewhere, London-based knitwear designer Oscar Ouyang has made a sweet little lamb a recurring signature, appearing on his whimsical knits and charming clothing labels. For her recent collaboration with Frankies Bikinis, Devon Lee Carlson joined forces with longtime friend Francesca Aiello to revisit treasured vintage pieces from their own wardrobes, complete with sweet pink co-branded labels decorated with a little dog and flowers. And in another corner of London, Sinéad O’Dwyer has been rethinking her brand identity as her customers grow up alongside her, with her newly imagined logo finding its way into the stitching on the back of her jeans.

For London-based demi-couture designer Ellie Misner, a clothing label can also serve as a little love letter commemorating a particularly special moment. Misner, who works on bespoke pieces, has taken to hand-embroidering her clients’s names above her own handwritten logo. For Raye, who fulfilled a long-held dream by headlining Reading and Leeds Festival, Misner stitched her name in burgundy thread into a crimson corseted gown. For Tems, whose Glastonbury main-stage performance marked another career milestone, it was a cobalt-blue signature sewn onto the inside of a midnight-blue ensemble. “My labels are my handwriting,” Misner tells Vogue, explaining that she handwrites the wearer’s name and then embroiders it, often choosing a thread that corresponds with the garment. For a performance that means so much to both artist and designer, it’s a way of marking the occasion, making the piece feel like more than just another custom commission. Misner likens the gesture to “a love note to their garment.” She adds: “I wish I could do it for everyone,” but the time-consuming process makes each one all the more special. These aren’t all bespoke gestures in the couture sense, but they share a certain spirit that insists on individuality, as well as the pleasure of details that one can keep entirely to oneself.

There’s something especially resonant about all this in an age of AI-generated images, algorithmically dictated taste, and increasingly impersonal consumption. Fashion, more and more, seems keen to remind us that there are actual people, with skills and emotions behind the clothes. At Chanel’s fall 2026 couture show, artist Joël Blanc painted the runway live in watercolors, capturing the spectacle in real time. And look at the new holiday campaigns from Prada, Dior, and Bottega Veneta, where all three have embraced the nostalgic charms of illustration and animation. Prada, in particular, has made a point of celebrating hand-drawn artistry, enlisting veteran animator John Pomeroy to conjure a whimsical winter wonderland populated by snow lynxes and mischievous mice.

In a world where almost anything can be reproduced, the idiosyncratic and intimate feel increasingly precious. The most meaningful thing about what we wear might be something nobody else can see.

#6544. 37 Family Dinner Ideas You’ll Make on Repeat

The good news about “family-friendly” dinners? They can be whatever you want them to be. Loaded sweet potato wedges eaten straight from the sheet pan? Absolutely. A dose of nostalgia by way of movie-night sloppy Joes, updated with a fiery kick of gochujang? No question about it. These are dinners for cautious eaters and adventurous ones alike—some familiar, some a little unexpected, and all worth bringing to the table.

Whether tonight calls for a cozy soup (that you can set and forget in your Instant Pot) or easy fish tacos (we have a hunch they’ll become part of your regular weeknight dinner rotation), we’ve got plenty of ideas to keep dinner interesting all year long.

Set tortillas, flaky cod or halibut, spicy lime sauce, and toppings out family-style and let everyone assemble their own piled-high tacos. It’s a simple weeknight family dinner that doubles as a choose-your-own-adventure activity.

Packed with ground chicken, white beans, and canned green chiles, this fast-cooking stew only gets better over time, so make a big batch. We promise, you won’t mind eating it two days in a row.

High-protein cottage cheese replaces often-pricier ricotta in this thrifty-ish spin on a familiar family favorite. More shocking: mozzarella is out too, in favor of tangy super-melter Fontina.

If your family loves pepperoni pizza, they’ll love this baked pasta, which hits all the saucy, spicy, cheesy notes with no takeout required. Roasting the sauce on a sheet pan concentrates its flavor before everything gets a blanket of cheese.

All the appeal of a spicy salmon roll, reassembled as a family-friendly bowl. Pickled cucumber and spicy mayo accompany crackly, broiled salmon cubes for a dinner that’s as fun to eat as it is easy to customize.

Smoky-sweet Korean gochujang lends a hum of heat to this riff on a childhood favorite. Soft buns and a stack of napkins do the rest.

Think chicken pot pie, but in cozy soup form. Complete with crackly, buttery shards of puff pastry you can tear and share, this family meal practically demands a crowd around the table.

This shareable skillet is packed with the flavors of a family-favorite appetizer, with roasted poblanos, red onions, and jalapeños smothered in cheesy sauce.

Store-bought pizza dough makes this family-friendly dinner a snap, even on busy weeknights. This California Pizza Kitchen-inspired recipe is smoky-sweet thanks to barbecue sauce, Gouda cheese, and frizzled mushrooms.

Store-bought zhug, a Yemeni-spiced cilantro sauce, and your broiler are the shortcuts to juicy, charred, baked chicken without a grill. It’s an easy, low-fuss dinner that delivers big flavor.

Somewhere between nachos and loaded potatoes, roasted sweet potatoes get topped with spiced ground beef and briny kimchi for a main dish that’s complete enough to enjoy straight off the sheet pan.

Genuinely juicy, supremely crispy, flavored like falafel, and browned in a skillet for ultimate ease. Serve them with your favorite burger toppings for an easy family dinner.

Sometimes you just want to cook an old faithful—the kind of dinner you know the whole family will love. That’s when you reach for this rich, cheesy, ever-reliable baked ziti.

These vibrant (and vegetarian) kale-and-black-bean-stuffed peppers are a repeat-worthy, one-dish dinner full of hearty flavor. Stirring a dollop of sour cream into the tomato sauce gives it rich texture.

Everyone loves a customizable dinner, and this shawarma-spiced chicken is made for it. Set out warm pitas and all your favorite fixings, like sliced tomatoes and cucumber spears, and let everyone build their perfect plate.

Shrimp cooked in garlicky, lemony butter is bound to be delicious. Serve it with crusty bread or toss it with pasta for a cozy weeknight meal the whole family will love.

Golden-edged tofu meets a bold, spicy satay-inspired peanut sauce in this quick, satisfying dish. Pile it over rice or serve with naan for scooping.

Canned pumpkin is good for way more than sweets. Here, lemon, Parmesan, and chile flakes turn it into a creamy, savory sauce that comes together while the pasta boils.

Spinach-packed dal is a lifesaver on nights when you’re strapped for time but craving something deeply comforting. Serve it with rice or flatbread for a quick vegetarian meal.

Tender soy-glazed chicken meatballs and crisp sesame green beans make a balanced family dinner that needs little else than a pot of rice.

Transform two favorite store-bought ingredients—cheese ravioli and crispy fried onions—into a rich and luscious skillet dinner with a crispy, savory top.

This sunny, dressed-for-summer family dinner relies on a pantry-friendly chicken marinade. All you need: sugar, vinegar, salt, and a few spices. Add couscous and dinner is done.

Make these succulent pork chops when it’s 6:26 p.m. on a Monday and you haven’t figured out what’s for dinner. The sweet-and-savory sauce makes this quick weeknight meal feel planned ahead.

Canned chickpeas and frozen broccoli keep this one-skillet dinner fast and thrifty, while cream cheese delivers on the faux pasta Alfredo front.

Leftover rice meets plenty of fresh ginger, soy sauce, and eggs in this satisfying 20-minute dinner. The key is starting with cold, cooked rice, which crisps up beautifully in a hot skillet.

Cherry tomatoes burst around a block of feta in the oven, forming a tangy, creamy pasta sauce. Calabrian chile paste brings a welcome kick that cuts through the richness.

This hearty catch-all skillet dinner tastes just as good in egg burritos the next morning, or make and freeze it up to three months ahead.

Upgrade grilled salmon with a punchy, vibrant dill chimichurri. It’s quick, fresh, and feels fancy enough to make you feel like you have your life together.

Much faster to make than risotto, this lemony, bright orzotto gets its herby savoriness from a pantry savior: store-bought jarred pesto.

Your favorite party dip, now in pasta form. Frozen spinach and jarred artichokes keep things convenient, while plenty of bubbling cheese makes this skillet dinner every bit as comforting as the original.

Crisp bibb lettuce leaves make the perfect cups for this spicy larb-inspired chicken, which you can dress up with fresh herbs and fried shallots. It’s a fun, hands-on family dinner that gets everyone involved.

This is the kind of salad that can hold its own as a family dinner, packed with roasted sweet potato and tofu, crisp red apple, and a bright, herby green goddess dressing.

#6543. GQ’s 2026 Men of the Year Party Brought Everyone Out

There’s no party quite like a GQ party. Who else could bring together Andrew Garfield, Robby Hoffman, Future, and Angel Reese under one roof? But that’s exactly what we did on Thursday night at Los Angeles’s famed Chateau Marmont for our 31st Men of the Year party, presented by Johnnie Walker Blue Label.

Following a dinner honoring our trio of cover stars—Matt Damon, Chris Rock, and Garfield—the real fun began when all three of them, along with nearly every other celebrity in town, descended on the Chateau’s garden to mix it up to the sounds of DJ Yung Tada (plus a late-night set from GQ Breakouts electro-pop duo Fcukers).

I caught Damon at the entrance to the party looking to continue our conversation from his cover story, but our reunion was cut short when Inde Navarette pulled up to say hi and exchange contacts. If the 25-year-old Obsession newcomer was starstruck by the 56-year-old Hollywood hero, the feeling seemed mutual.

Future and Travis Scott rolled up nearly at the same time; Travis, who performed the end-credits track for The Odyssey, told me he was ready to hit the Oscars campaign trail.

In every corner was a cluster of stars from different Hollywood galaxies. Abbott Elementary’s Tyler James Williams and Chris Perfetti made the rounds together, looking nothing like the harried teachers they play on TV. GQ Breakout Owen Thiele and his longtime friend Cazzie David (who gave Owen his first acting gig on her web series years ago) ignored our red carpet instructions to bless us with photogenic poses they’d pre-planned long in advance. When I asked broadcaster Taylor Rooks for an on-the-fly NBA Cup prediction, she gushed about the Celtics and the Lakers. And there was something fun about seeing Anderson .Paak and Diplo chop it up, too.

The friendly embrace shared by Austin Abrams and Skyler Gisondo, noted Good Dudes, is the unscripted team-up the internet goes nuts for. The Resident Evil and Primetime actors later shared that they’d just been on the phone together while getting ready for the party, neither realizing they’d be seeing each other shortly. When I brought up James Gunn and his recent departure from DC Studios, Gisondo called it a “bummer”—he just wrapped the “Jimmy Olsen vs. Gorilla Grodd” series, he said, and hopes that it’ll still come out (and that Gunn continues to write and direct even if he’s not in executive mode anymore).

In other unlikely but endearing encounters: Ayo Edebiri and Thiele excitedly nabbed IShowSpeed for a photo, and Lamorne Morris stopped Anthony Ippolito to give him props for I Play Rocky, counseling him to take it all in. Ippolito told me he’s headed off to Europe soon to continue promoting the film; a certified foodie, he was hunting for Paris recs (I had to put him on to HolyBelly, for the pancakes). I also caught GQ’s Director of the Year Denis Villeneuve, whose eyes lit up when I mentioned his woefully underrated Jake Gyllenhaal thriller Enemy.

Midway through the night I spotted Andrew Garfield and Monica Barbaro, who were considering an Irish exit. #6542. Gravy-Braised Turkey

Cooking a whole turkey is a commitment. Between the schlepping, trussing, and constant babysitting, it’s a serious investment—and one that doesn’t always pay dividends. For a more laid-back affair, and one that practically guarantees success, might we suggest turkey legs cooked directly in gravy? Yes, in the gravy.

This recipe will defy everything you have probably done to cook a turkey until now. The first important step is searing the whole turkey legs for optimal browning. Now you are ready to create a base for the gravy with all those drippings and toasty bits left in the pot. No need to make a full-on roux either: Just sprinkle in the flour over the melted fat, whisk to combine, and slowly pour in the broth. Once the gravy is done, in goes the turkey and aromatics for braising. The rest is you worrying about something else, because that turkey will cook itself.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 325°. Season 4 whole turkey legs (thigh and drumstick; about 6½ lb. total), patted dry, all over with kosher salt and freshly ground pepper. Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large braiser or Dutch oven over medium-high. Working in 2 batches if needed to avoid overcrowding, arrange turkey legs, skin side down, in pot and cook, undisturbed, rotating pan on burner a few times to ensure even browning, until browned underneath and they easily release from pot, 8–12 minutes. Transfer turkey legs to a rimmed baking sheet, arranging skin side up. (No need to brown other side; turkey will still be raw at this point.)

Add more oil if pot looks dry; arrange 2 large oranges and/or lemons, halved, and 2 heads of garlic, tops trimmed to expose cloves, cut side down in pot and add 3 large shallots, peeled. Cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 2–3 minutes. Transfer each to baking sheet with turkey as they are done (it’s okay if some fall apart slightly).

Add 6 Tbsp. (¾ stick) unsalted butter to pot and cook until melted. Sprinkle in ⅓ cup (42 g) all-purpose flour and cook, stirring constantly, until no pockets of dry flour remain, about 1 minute. Gradually pour in 4 cups low-sodium chicken broth, stirring constantly to combine. Bring to a simmer and cook until gravy is just starting to thicken, about 2 minutes. Stir in 3 Tbsp. Worcestershire sauce and season with salt and pepper.

Nestle turkey legs into gravy, skin side up, then tuck oranges, garlic, and shallots around, arranging oranges and garlic cut side up. Add 1 small bunch thyme (about 10 sprigs), tied with kitchen twine, and cover pot tightly with a lid or foil. Braise 2 hours. (If your pot is too small to comfortably fit everything, transfer gravy to a 13x9" baking dish before adding turkey legs and aromatics.) Uncover pot and continue to bake until turkey legs are deeply browned, meat shreds easily off the bone, and gravy has thickened a little, 45–55 minutes.

Let turkey and gravy cool slightly before serving. Transfer to a platter if desired. (If gravy has excess fat on top, skim off with a spoon and discard before serving or spooning over legs on platter.)

#6541. 44 Best Wedding Guest Dresses in 2026 for Every Type of Ceremony

Once you’ve coordinated your wedding guest schedule, the next step is figuring out what to wear to all those nuptials. Between decoding dress codes (just how casual is a “casual” wedding, really?) and navigating different climates, you’ll quickly realize there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to this sort of occasion styling. So if you find yourself in the run-up to a fancy affair with a closet full of not-quite-right frocks and a looming deadline—don’t panic. We pulled together an edit of the best wedding guest dresses to suit every possible style, venue, and budget.

While some eveningwear requirements are set in stone, many leave room for creativity depending on the wedding theme. For instance: A black-tie ceremony does necessitate floor-length gowns—but that doesn’t mean a fuchsia-hued dress is off the table. A spring or summer wedding might have you gravitating toward sleeveless silhouettes and airier fabrics in the name of practicality, so why not pick a rich color like chartreuse or cerulean for an unexpected twist on the palette of the season? And while a cocktail dress code or daytime fête definitely suggests more laid-back attire, there’s plenty of opportunity to stand out with the details—think, a lace-trimmed midi or a tiger stripe-inspired number.

Whatever’s in the cards (we mean this literally—please read the invite carefully), our picks for the best wedding guest dresses cover a lot of ground.

The coldest days of the year come with the quandary of formal dressing for freezing temps (is there anything worse than having to cover a great dress with a puffer coat?). Stay warm in Staud’s long-sleeve maxi or a velvet option by Veronica Beard. Or, fully embrace winter glam in Simkhai’s halterneck gown, which has a low back for some drama.

Formal weddings are your moment to go all out with dramatic lengths and unexpected draping. Labels like Victoria Beckham, Fforme, and L’Agence show us how it’s done—just don’t forget the right jewels for a finishing touch.

Spring nuptials call for soft hues—though we’re all for trying a zippier take on pastels. H&M’s floral jacquard maxi dress in light turquoise will get you in the mood for a garden affair, while Totême’s soft pink midi pretty much works for any venue, as far as we’re concerned.

Toast the new couple in a spirited cocktail dress. COS’s gray midi delivers modern Art Deco glamour, while Ralph Lauren’s mock-neck style is all easy elegance. Then there’s Diotima’s LBD, a halterneck design bound to become a closet staple for future events.

Attending a courthouse ceremony or a more intimate backyard celebration? Elevated comfort is the name of the game. Slip on something easygoing with a modern finish—like Blaze Milano’s satin dress in a golden hue—or go for a more striking, unexpected piece from Tory Burch for a look that’s both playful and polished.

The best way to bring personality to a dress code with a limited palette? Play with silhouette and texture. Aje keeps things party-ready with fringe detailing; Kallmeyer brings evening elegance with a floor-length hem; and Banana Republic’s high-neck, long-sleeve option suits wintry affairs well.

This is one prompt that eliminates the guesswork; plus, you can never go wrong with a romantic bloom, no matter the silhouette. Keep accessories simple (sleek kitten heels and minimalist jewelry are the right choice here) and let the pattern do all the work.

From Italian villas to rolling countrysides, the best way to go about a destination wedding is to take notes from your surroundings. Lean into the romance of a cobblestoned town with a silky, lace-trimmed dress from Simon Miller, or buy into the breezy style of an island venue with Christopher John Rogers’ striped crinkle-chiffon gown.

Bold citrus hues and sultry silks define the mood for summer wedding dressing, we say—and Aflalo and Tove are both on board. For a more formal option, Taller Marmo’s one-shoulder gown with a fringe-trimmed cape will make you the best-dressed guest.

A shoreside ceremony is your cue to relax a little. Lighter-weight fabrics and simple silhouettes are fair game, especially when you play with texture and pattern. Coastal shades and sun-washed hues feel perfectly at home here, too. Style yours with open-toed sandals and nautical-inspired accessories, and you’re good to go.

Autumn wedding season calls for dresses in a deep, rich palette. La Ligne’s long-sleeve design in navy and Anine Bing’s modern slip in burgundy both offer universally flattering colors, while Maria McManus’s lace bodice dress and Dries Van Noten’s floral midi are splashier options for those with an affinity for details. Complete the look with a silk wrap draped around your shoulders once temperatures dip after cocktail hour.

When in doubt, let the season lead—jewel tones and deep neutrals for fall and winter, and soft pastels or vibrant hues for spring and summer. Be sure to also check the invitation and wedding website, as some couples may ask guests to dress within a color palette, and it’s important you honor their wishes.

What colors should I avoid as a wedding guest?

If you remember anything, remember this: Steer clear of white, ivory, and anything that could read as bridal, unless the couple says otherwise. Keep cultural customs in mind, too, as red and black are off-limits at some ceremonies. Again, if you’re unsure, check the invitation or wedding website, or ask a member of the bridal party for guidance.

How do I know what style and silhouette to wear?

The dress code, venue, season, and time of day should guide your choices. Here’s a quick rundown: Floor-length for black tie, knee- to midi-length for semi-formal and cocktail, minis for more casual celebrations, airy silhouettes for outdoor, beach, or daytime affairs, and thicker fabrics for the cooler months. And don’t forget about your accessories, whether that’s block heels for a lawn ceremony or a shawl for a more conservative house of worship.

How do I find a dress that works for multiple weddings?

If you have several weddings on the horizon, opt for a look in a solid hue and an easygoing shape, like a sheath style or handkerchief hemline. These pieces are extremely versatile, easier to rewear than trend-driven prints, and simple to restyle with different shoes, jewelry, and outerwear.

#6540. 3 Ways To Defrost Chicken Without Spreading Salmonella, According To An Expert

Your dinner plans aren't ruined just yet.

Forgetting to take chicken out of the freezer is an all-too-common occurrence that can bring your dinner plans to a screeching halt. To get things back on track, your gut instinct may be to thaw it as quickly as possible. But there are more important things to worry about than a delayed dinner.

Raw poultry can carry Salmonella, so how you handle it matters. Nothing is less appetizing than giving your whole family a foodborne illness.

But before you give up and order takeout, we’re here to help. We chatted with Ellen Steinberg, PhD, RD, LD, and food safety specialist, to find the best (and safest) methods to thaw chicken. Whether you plan ahead or need to defrost it fast, here’s what you should do.

Defrosting chicken isn’t as simple as taking it out of the freezer. Salmonella is real, y’all—according to FoodSafety.gov, roughly 4% of chicken packages at American grocery stores are contaminated with the bacteria. That bacteria can multiply rapidly in the temperature danger zone, between 40°F and 140°F. Translation: Leaving your chicken out on the counter can actually make you sick.

To prevent that, choose the right method and protect the surrounding environment from cross-contamination. Even with supposedly airtight packaging, the plastic may have holes, or chicken juice may transfer from other packages at the grocery store. It’s especially difficult to spot when the meat is frozen, so Steinberg says it’s better to be safe than sorry.

“You should put your [raw] chicken in a roasting pan or a baking sheet so the juices won’t spread,” she says. Everything that touches raw chicken should be thoroughly cleaned with hot, soapy water. If you want to take food safety even further, Steinberg suggests keeping a separate cutting board in a different color that you use exclusively for raw meat. And above all else: Wash your hands!

If you’re not in a rush, thawing chicken in the fridge yields the most consistent results. Because refrigerators should stay at 40°F and below, frozen chicken can gradually defrost without entering the temperature danger zone where bacteria multiply more rapidly.

Because of this, Steinberg says it’s the only USDA-approved thawing method that lets you refreeze raw chicken without cooking it first. “If you end up deciding that you don’t want to cook the chicken or you only want to use half of it, you can place it back in the freezer,” she says. There is a caveat, however: Once your chicken has fully thawed, you should either cook or refreeze it within one to two days.

If you opt for the refrigerator method, keep these safety measures in mind. Beyond keeping your meat contained on a plate or tray, place it on the bottom shelf. If juice drips, it’ll contaminate the fewest ingredients. Steinberg also suggests storing the chicken toward the back of your refrigerator. “The temperature is more consistent, unlike the areas closest to the door,” she says.

If you need to defrost chicken fast, one of the best ways is with cool, running water. Unlike fridge air, water conducts heat much more effectively. Keeping the water moving also helps maintain consistent thawing conditions. But you don't necessarily need to leave the faucet running: The USDA also recommends submerging chicken in cold water and changing it every 30 minutes.

So if cold water thaws meat quickly, would hot water do the job even faster? It might, but the potential food safety risks aren't worth it. "If you thaw chicken under warm or hot water, the outside of the meat can enter the temperature danger zone while the center is still frozen,” Steinberg says.

For the running-water method, place the chicken in leak-proof packaging in a bowl and run cool water (70°F or lower) over it. Thawing times depend on the size and thickness of the meat, but smaller packages may be ready in an hour or less. Once thawed, cook the chicken immediately before considering refreezing it.

The final USDA-approved method involves using your microwave’s defrost setting. While it’s certainly faster than letting meat thaw in the fridge, we suggest relying on this method only if you have no other option.

Steinberg says this technique leaves the least wiggle room for planning your dinner. “You have to cook it immediately,” she says. “You can’t defrost it and then decide to cook two hours later.”

The need to cook immediately is certainly one downside of the microwave method. However, another compelling argument against using the defrost setting is that it can make your chicken taste worse.

Microwaves heat food unevenly, especially with thicker pieces of meat. Some areas can start warming up or even cooking before the center fully thaws. It's not a big deal when reheating leftovers, but it can nearly ruin frozen proteins.

By the time the center is fully defrosted, the outer edges may already be partially cooked. Can you imagine chicken that tastes worse than unseasoned microwaved chicken? We can't.

It’s a safe and fast defrosting method when followed by immediate cooking—but at what cost? So we'd only vouch for this technique if your chicken will end up shredded or submerged in enough sauce to mask the texture.

#6539. Bon Appétit Pick: HelloFresh Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls

Over the past few years, BA editors have tested just about every meal delivery service out there, and HelloFresh keeps standing out for its bold flavors. To choose them, we cooked many, many kits in our home kitchens and in the BA Test Kitchen, following the recipe cards exactly. We judged each one on flavor, portion size, cook time, cuisine variety, and the recipe's step-by-step clarity. This Ginger Chicken and Rice Bowl is one of those picks. Here’s what it’s like to make it at home.

As a product tester, I'm very methodical, so I was excited to help build the BA Picks collection. I got to cook a bunch of meals and decide which ones were the best—the same process I take when testing the best pizza ovens or juicers. Despite being Italian, I'm constantly drawn to Asian flavors when I cook at home on weeknights. The balance of salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic is highly addictive. It hits the spot after a long day of reviewing appliances in the Test Kitchen.

That's why the Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls caught my eye. Made with soy, Thai chili sauce, gochujang, ponzu, and Korean chili flakes, it has all the flavors I crave. It reminded me of some of my favorite BA recipes, like our Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry, a mainstay in my weeknight rotation. Can a meal kit recipe stand up to a Bon Appétit recipe that's tested over weeks of development? It was my job to find out. (Spoiler alert: It did.)

HelloFresh's Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls pair saucy ginger chicken with rice, a spicy cucumber side, and toasted peanuts on top. The recipe card rates it easy and lists a total time of 20 minutes. You can order it in two-, three-, four-, or six-serving sizes.

I have an entire container in my fridge dedicated to Asian condiments. If I were cooking this recipe from scratch, I'd have to lug the whole thing out, and the bottles would cover my counter. HelloFresh measures everything out for you, so all you have to do is open the bags and follow the step-by-step instructions.

This kit came with a "mini" cucumber that was more like a normal-size one (perfect for me, since I love cucumber salad). It also had all the seasonings, rice, toppings like peanuts, and chopped chicken breast.

The pre-chopped chicken was the underrated MVP. I rarely cook chicken at home because I hate handling it raw, plus the cleanup that comes after. (Always sanitize your cutting board and prep station after working with raw meat!) So HelloFresh came in clutch here. The only ingredients I had to pull from my own pantry were oil, salt, pepper, and a small dash of sugar.

HelloFresh instructions include photos of each step, so they're easy to follow. I started by putting a pot of rice on. Then I chopped and salted the cucumbers so they could season while I cooked the chicken. After a quick sauté in a pan, I tossed the chicken in the sauce, and it was ready. Once I drained the cucumbers, all I had to do was add the chili flakes, gochujang, sesame oil, ponzu, and sugar. From start to finish, the whole process took me all of 20 minutes. That was great, because the smells coming from each component were making my mouth water.

This dish exceeded my expectations for a meal kit. The cucumbers got a ton of umami from the fermented gochujang dressing, and the chicken was saucy, with a punch of ponzu. The ginger sauce has it all: a sweet, mild ginger flavor, a trace of salty soy, and a hint of heat. Thai chili sauce and ponzu turn it into a sticky glaze for the chicken. The cucumbers add a cooling side and a pop of color, and the peanuts on top are the finishing touch. These are flavors I'd never expect in a delivery box, and I'm super impressed.

Anyone looking to explore Asian ingredients would learn a lot from this dish. It uses gochujang, ponzu, Thai chili sauce, and Korean chili flakes. I'd never cooked with Korean chili flakes (also known as gochugaru), so I was excited to taste it. If you want a quick dinner, this recipe comes together in just 20 minutes. It's a flavorful dish without project-level effort.

The Ginger Chicken & Rice Bowls hit the salty, sweet, spicy, and acidic balance I crave after a long day. The pre-chopped chicken and photo-guided steps make it easy, and there's no counter full of condiments to put away afterward. Find it in the BA Picks collection on HelloFresh, along with an exclusive three-month digital subscription to Bon Appétit.

#6538. Buttered Nut Squash

We rate butternut the most affable winter squash—relatively easy to prepare, consistently delicious, and available at most grocery stores. The buttered nut dressing is more than just cheeky wordplay. Bold from brown butter and balsamic vinegar and bright from lemon, the crunchy topping is an excellent foil to the sweetness of roasted squash. Cook the squash a couple hours ahead of time and all you’ll have left to do before dinner is make the dressing.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Place a rack in lower third of oven; preheat to 425°. Lightly crush 2 tsp. fennel seeds with a mortar and pestle or place on a cutting board and gently crush with a heavy pan. Peel 1 medium butternut squash (about 3 lb.) and halve lengthwise. Scoop out seeds; discard. Cut squash into 2" irregular pieces, aiming for sharp, jagged shapes. Transfer to a large rimmed baking sheet; drizzle with 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with fennel seeds, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 1 tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Toss squash to coat, arrange in a single layer, and roast until browned and tender, 30–35 minutes.

Do Ahead: Squash can be roasted 2 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

While the squash is roasting, cook 6 oz. thick-cut bacon, cut into 1" pieces, in a medium skillet over medium heat, stirring often, until browned and mostly crisp, 8–12 minutes. Transfer to a small plate with a slotted spoon.

Reduce heat to low; combine 1 cup raw pecans and 4 Tbsp. unsalted butter in same pan. Cook, stirring often, until butter browns and nuts have slightly darkened, 6–8 minutes. Remove from heat. Stir in 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped (this will give it a head start to take off the raw edge), then add bacon, zest and juice of 1 large lemon, 3 sprigs sage, and 2 Tbsp. balsamic vinegar and stir to combine. Taste dressing and season with kosher salt if needed.

Arrange squash on a platter and spoon dressing over.
